CO2018M-P1-41.exp: Radio buttons are grouped so only one can be selected at a time, making the options mutually exclusive; check boxes, by contrast, allow multiple simultaneous selections.

CO2018M-P1-42.exp: In the classic Windows Start menu, Disk Cleanup lives under All Programs > Accessories > System Tools > Disk Cleanup, a maintenance utility grouped with other system tools.

CO2018M-P1-43.exp: The wildcard *.EXE (with the dot) is what tells DIR to match the .EXE extension specifically; option B drops the dot so *EXE would not correctly isolate the extension field. The missing space before *.EXE in option C looks like a printing/OCR slip rather than a genuine alternative command.

CO2018M-P1-44.exp: The standard ATTRIB trick taught for hiding a folder sets both the system and hidden attributes together (+s +h), which is the combination this question bank consistently treats as the 'hide' command; +h alone would also hide it, but that option isn't offered.

CO2018M-P1-45.exp: Word documents save as .doc in the older binary format (Word 97-2003) or .docx in the modern XML-based format introduced with Word 2007, so both are correct default extensions depending on version.

CO2018M-P1-46.exp: Ctrl+S is the standard Save shortcut across Microsoft Office applications, including Word.

CO2018M-P1-47.exp: The Home key moves the cursor to the start of the current line; End moves to the end of the line, and Page Up/Down scroll by screen rather than moving within a line.

CO2018M-P1-48.exp: Word offers four paragraph alignments: Left, Center, Right, and Justify.

CO2018M-P1-49.exp: AutoCorrect is the Word feature that automatically fixes common typing and spelling mistakes as you type (e.g., 'teh' to 'the').

CO2018M-P1-50.exp: Mail Merge combines a standard document (like a letter) with a data source of names and addresses to produce personalized copies for each recipient.

CO2018M-P1-51.exp: The toolbar holds icon buttons for frequently used commands (save, print, formatting, etc.) for one-click access, unlike the menu bar which requires navigating dropdown lists.

CO2018M-P1-52.exp: Ctrl+Right Arrow jumps the cursor forward one word at a time; moving to end of line or document requires End or Ctrl+End instead.

CO2018M-P1-53.exp: Ctrl+G opens the Find and Replace dialog box with its Go To tab already active, letting you jump to a specific page, line, or bookmark; there is no separate standalone 'Go To' dialog outside this shared box.

CO2018M-P1-54.exp: Print Preview renders the document exactly as it will appear on the printed page, including page breaks, margins, and graphics placement, which Normal or Web Layout views do not accurately show.

CO2018M-P1-55.exp: Format Painter copies the exact formatting of selected text and applies it to newly selected text with one click; retyping text or using Paste Special does not reliably replicate formatting the same way, so 'All of these' is not accurate.

CO2018M-P1-56.exp: A Word table can have a maximum of 63 columns, a longstanding limit carried through modern versions of Word.

CO2018M-P1-57.exp: Older Excel documentation and the textbooks this question is drawn from cite 255 as the maximum number of worksheets a workbook can contain; later Excel versions relaxed this to be limited mainly by available memory, but 255 is the figure this exam-prep tradition uses.

CO2018M-P1-58.exp: For backward compatibility with older spreadsheet programs like Lotus 1-2-3, Excel accepts a formula entry starting with either '=' or '+', though it internally normalizes it to start with '='.

CO2018M-P1-59.exp: Excel defaults to relative referencing, so cell references in a copied formula shift automatically based on the new location; absolute referencing must be explicitly requested with '$' signs.

CO2018M-P1-60.exp: A dollar sign ($) placed before the column letter and/or row number locks (makes absolute) that part of the reference so it doesn't change when the formula is copied elsewhere.
